newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian minister faces growing pressure to quit.
newsitem.headline: Australian minister faces growing pressure to quit.

text.p: The Australian Government faced mounting pressure on Tuesday to sack Small Business Minister Geoff Prosser over controversy surrounding his business interests.
Government sources said back benchers were increasingly concerned at the damage the scandal was causing the government and believed Prosser's future was limited.
"It's just a few of the comments when I've spoken with (some back benchers) and it's their opinion that he dosen't have long to go," a government source told Reuters.
The Labor oppositon has demanded Australian Prime Minister John Howard sack Prosser, accusing him of misleading parliament, breaching ministerial standards and a possible conflict of interest.
Howard has already narrowed the portfolio of Prosser, a businessman who owns shopping malls in Western Australia.

Opposition leader Kim Beazley has critisised the prime minister for failing to deal with the situation before leaving on a 16 day trip to the United Kingdom and the United States of America a week ago.
"Any other government that was led by somebody other than a very weak prime minister would have dealt with this minister ages ago," Beasley told reporters on Tuesday.
Government guidelines bar ministers from daily business activities and from being involved in decisions which could affect their business interests.
The opposition has accused Prosser of understating the extent of his dealings with leading businessman and former senior conservative politician Nick Greiner.

On Monday, Prosser admitted to Parliament that he had talked with Greiner about the possibility of opening a Target discount department store in one of his three Western Australian shopping malls, after earlier refusing to answer questions.
But he has denied any wrong-doing.
Howard, who vowed to improved parliamentary standards when he was elected in March 1996, has been plagued by a series of scandals involving his ministers and back benchers.

A junior minister and a parliamentary secretary quit last year after allegations of potential conflict of interest, and one government member and a recently retired government senator are before the courts on charges of abusing parliamentary benefits.
